upstream_choice.alternatives_considered: ikatyang/tree-sitter-toml (58 stars, last pushed 2024-05-01) is the ANCESTOR of the pinned repo, not a rival: tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-toml is its continuation and still credits Ika as author. It owns neither the nvim nor the Helix pin, and its crates.io name tree-sitter-toml now points at a third party (Mathspy/tree-sitter-toml, 185,023 downloads all-time, 27,783 in 90 days) — 7.6x fewer all-time and 24.9x fewer recent than the pinned grammar. Zed LOOKS like a third opinion and is not: zed-extensions/toml pins tree-sitter/tree-sitter-toml @ 342d9be, which is an ARCHIVED FORK of ikatyang last pushed 2022-04-21, 10 stars. Recorded because 'all three editors' in the ROADMAP would otherwise imply three live pins; there are two, and they agree exactly.
upstream_choice.staleness_note: docs/data/grammar-health-2026-08-10.tsv records this repo at 395 days since push. Its DEFAULT BRANCH has not moved in 617 days: master HEAD is 64b56832, dated 2024-12-03, and the 2025-07-10 push that days_since_push measures went to a side branch named `update`. GitHub's pushed_at counts any branch. ROADMAP section 3's stale-grammar analysis is built on days_since_push and therefore reads every repo with a live side branch and a dead default branch as healthier than it is. Stated here rather than as a ROADMAP edit because six sessions were editing that file concurrently.

generate_cli_note: same pin as the other grammars: tree-sitter-cli 0.26.x ships broken Unicode identifier tables (see treebank-rust ledger)
generate_deps_note: null, verified rather than assumed: grammar.js contains no require() of another grammar, so generation needs no node_modules. The package.json devDependency on tree-sitter-cli is upstream's own tooling and is not what generate_deps is for.

oracle.tool: the `toml` crate's toml::Table parse, in-process, driven by rayon
oracle.note: TWO-VALUED: valid / invalid. In-process like treebank-rust's syn, so there is no fork and no stdin protocol. Parsing to a Table rather than to a syntax tree is not an optimisation choice, it is the only honest stage: duplicate keys, a table redefined over a key, a dotted-key conflict and a calendar-invalid datetime (2024-02-30) are all SPEC-level invalid TOML, not a later type-check, so a syntax-only TOML parser silently accepts about a dozen classes of invalid TOML. That is exactly the treebank-php trap and the reason `stage` is recorded.
oracle.unreadable_note: An unreadable file is NOT an invalid file: the oracle writes the path and the OS error to stderr and exits 1 rather than emitting a verdict. Ill-formed UTF-8 IS a verdict (invalid), not an I/O failure, because the bytes arrived intact and TOML 1.1.0 requires the document be valid UTF-8 — see driver_owns_utf8 below. Direction of failure, which matters more than the fact of handling it: this oracle fails CLOSED. Anything it cannot decode is called invalid, which books as corpus noise, so the worst case is an understated gap count and never a fix agent dispatched at a file nothing can parse.
oracle.driver_owns_utf8: toml::Table implements FromStr only — the crate has no bytes-taking entry point — so the driver decodes and therefore owns one spec rule: UTF-8 well-formedness, via str::from_utf8. Audited rather than assumed, by feeding the crate already-valid &str and watching where verdicts come from. The crate owns ALL BOM handling and gets it right unaided: leading BOM valid, BOM-only document valid, mid-stream BOM invalid, doubled BOM invalid, BOM inside a basic string treated as content — matching toml-test's utf8-bom-01/02 and bom-not-at-start-01/02/03. UTF-16 rejection falls out of the UTF-8 rule without the driver naming UTF-16 at all. DO NOT strip a leading BOM in the driver: it looks like an improvement, it is what a js-yaml-shaped oracle genuinely needs, and here it would turn a doubled BOM into a leading one and silently flip an invalid file to valid. Recorded as a don't because it is exactly the tidying a later agent would do unprompted.

considered.why_not: identical verdicts; toml::Table is the more obvious call and no cheaper stage is honest

identical verdicts. Checked because it is the LSP-shaped parse and the one most likely to have error recovery; it does not. That all three stages coincide is why `stage` here records a checked non-choice rather than a lever.

populations.blind_to: BOM, ill-formed UTF-8, NUL, lone CR and tab indentation — measured zeros, all of them; a zero here is not reassurance

populations.name: toml-test, 1.0.0 vs 1.1.0 expectations

considered.why_not: REJECTED, and the reasoning is the load-bearing decision in this ledger — see spec_revision_choice below. Scores 709/709 against the 1.0.0 expectations, i.e. it is an exact 1.0.0 parser, and it is the safer-looking choice because it produces 3 gap files against this grammar where 1.1.4 produces 18. That is the wrong thing to optimise.

REJECTED on a defect, not on spec: it rejects a leading UTF-8 BOM, which TOML permits and toml-test encodes as valid (utf8-bom-01/02). All three of its encoding-battery failures are that one bug. Over-rejecting hides gaps as noise. Also 0.43 s/1000 against 0.053.

populations.name: toml-test 1.0.0
populations.how_measured: one process per file, verdict from exit status

considered.why_not: DISQUALIFIED, and NOT on speed — that has to be said explicitly because the obvious objection is wrong here. Parallelized the way lang::exec_oracle already runs php and bash, taplo is 0.78 s/1000 at 16 workers (14.1 serial), firmly Tier A. It fails on two other things. (1) Conformance: 698/709, of which 2 are accepts-invalid (table/append-with-dotted-keys-04, table/super-twice) and 9 are rejects-valid (BOM x2, non-ASCII in comments/keys/strings, uppercase float exponent, date-like keys, datetime edge). (2) Fatal: `taplo lint` takes GLOBS, so a path matching nothing collects zero files and EXITS 0. A directory does the same. Under exec_oracle status 0 means valid, so a mistyped corpus root would call every file valid, turn every grammar failure into a GAP, and dispatch a fix agent at each. GRAMMARS.md states this defect in the opposite polarity — mistyped root, everything invalid, gap_files falls to zero, flawless grammar — and exec_oracle's reject_statuses catches a tool that spells rejection with an unexpected status but structurally cannot catch a tool that spells 'I found nothing to check' as 0. This is the more expensive direction of the same defect and, on its own, disqualifying.

oracle_why_reference_and_not_position: authority is `reference` and the `position` block is deliberately absent. TOML has ONE authority — toml-lang — and no dispute about who decides, which is what separates it from treebank-yaml, where libyaml, go-yaml, PyYAML and snakeyaml genuinely disagree and the choice is a stated position rather than a fact. What TOML has instead is TWO RELEASED SPEC REVISIONS, and that is a `spec` question, not an `authority` one. The two fields were designed together with the tbyaml session precisely so this case could be expressed without bending either: the boring case should look boring.

spec_revision_choice.summary: TOML 1.1.0, not 1.0.0. This is the single most consequential field in this ledger and the reasoning inverts the obvious one.
spec_revision_choice.the_two_specs: TOML 1.0.0 released 2021-01-12; TOML 1.1.0 released 2025-12-24. Both are final releases of toml-lang/toml. 1.1.0 adds: seconds optional in times, linebreaks inside inline tables, trailing commas in inline tables, \e and \x escapes in basic strings.
spec_revision_choice.tools_have_already_split: The `toml` crate is 1.1.0 from 0.9 onward and 1.0.0 at 0.8; taplo 0.10.0 and CPython tomllib are 1.0.0. Measured against toml-test: toml 1.1.4 scores 712/712 on the 1.1.0 expectations and 700/709 on the 1.0.0 ones, its 9 divergences being exactly the 1.1.0 additions; toml 0.8.23 scores 709/709 on 1.0.0 and 701/712 on 1.1.0.
spec_revision_choice.version_string_trap: toml 0.9.9 ships on crates.io as literally `0.9.9+spec-1.0.0` and is NOT a 1.0.0 parser — measured, it accepts all nine 1.1.0-only constructs and scores 712/712 against the 1.1.0 expectations. The build metadata is stale. Never read a spec revision off a package version string. 0.8.23 is the last exact 1.0.0 line.
spec_revision_choice.why_not_the_safer_looking_1_0_0: A 1.0.0 oracle produces 3 gap files against this grammar over the 777-file conformance suite; a 1.1.0 oracle produces 18. Optimising for the smaller number would be exactly the drift GRAMMARS.md warns about, because the 15 extra are NOT phantom: this grammar genuinely does not implement TOML 1.1.0 (its own README targets v1.0.0, and it rejects 7 of the 9 divergent constructs). DESIGN.md exists because grammars fall behind; pinning the oracle to the superseded spec is the one choice that guarantees the sweep can never say so. Second and independent: under a 1.0.0 oracle the 1.1.0 constructs become ELIGIBLE for test/negative/, since the oracle rejects them and the grammar rejects them, which is the entry criterion. test/negative holds files the grammar must KEEP rejecting — so a later agent could legitimately add `a = { b = 1, }` there and cement this grammar at 1.0.0, making a future upgrade fail CI. Pinning 1.0.0 does not merely fail to surface the gap, it builds the mechanism to lock it in. Under 1.1.0 those constructs are oracle-valid and therefore structurally barred from test/negative.
spec_revision_choice.cost_today: Zero. On the 1427-file real corpus the two oracles agree on every file, gap_files is 0 under both, and the grammar parses 1427/1427 clean. The choice costs nothing measurable today and only starts to matter as 1.1.0 adoption appears in published packages — at which point it is the difference between the sweep reporting a real, bounded, correct work item and the sweep saying nothing.

grammar_is_narrower_than_the_oracle.summary: The inverse of treebank-lua's grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle, and it must be read as the DANGEROUS direction rather than the safe one. Lua's grammar accepts a superset of what its oracle calls valid, which can never manufacture a gap. This grammar accepts a SUBSET: it targets TOML 1.0.0 while the oracle is 1.1.0, so every 1.1.0-only construct is 'grammar rejects AND oracle says valid', which is the definition of a gap.
grammar_is_narrower_than_the_oracle.measured: Verified by parsing, not by reading upstream's README. Of the 9 constructs that separate the specs, the grammar REJECTS 7 — inline-table linebreak x4, inline-table trailing comma, local-time without seconds, \x byte escapes — and ACCEPTS 2 (offset and local datetimes without seconds, because its rfc3339_time regex is looser than the spec it claims). Over the 777-file union of the toml-test manifests: 18 gap / 368 noise / 132 grammar-broader / 259 clean against the 1.1.0 oracle, against 3 / 383 / 137 / 254 for a 1.0.0 oracle. The 15-file difference is enumerated in the sweep notes.
grammar_is_narrower_than_the_oracle.this_is_intended: These gaps are the system working, not numbers to tune away. The correct response to any of them appearing in a real package is a grammar patch bringing tree-sitter-toml up to TOML 1.1.0 — a coherent, bounded, upstreamable change of roughly four rules — and NOT a reclassification to noise or a swap of the oracle back to 1.0.0.
grammar_is_narrower_than_the_oracle.negative_corpus_consequence: test/negative/ must contain ONLY syntax invalid in BOTH revisions. No 1.1.0-only construct may appear there: the oracle calls them valid, so they are barred by the entry criterion, and putting them there would freeze this grammar at 1.0.0. Same rule treebank-lua reached about LuaJIT literals, arrived at from the opposite side.
grammar_is_narrower_than_the_oracle.second_axis_semantic_rules: As with lua, the oracle also rejects a class of files the grammar accepts and by its nature cannot reject: duplicate keys, a table redefined over a key, dotted-key conflicts, and calendar-invalid datetimes are semantic, not syntactic. This runs in the SAFE direction — grammar accepts, oracle rejects — so it cannot manufacture a gap, but it bounds test/negative further: a negative test may only use a pure syntax error, never a semantic one, because the grammar will not reject the latter.

oracle_cost: 0.053 s per 1000 files serial and 0.006 s per 1000 at 16 rayon workers, measured on 1427 real .toml files (3.73 MB) replayed 10x to get past timer resolution; process startup is unmeasurable (0.00 s) because the oracle is in-process. Throughput 48 MB/s serial. State that number WITH the corpus shape, because for a config language seconds-per-1000-FILES is a bytes/second measurement in disguise: mean 2.55 KB, median 1.59 KB. On go-sized files (22.9 KB mean) the same code would read ~0.5 s/1000. The reject path — every file truncated to 60%, which is the input validate() actually sees — is 0.022 s/1000, ~2.4x FASTER than the valid path, the same bail-at-first-error shape rust's syn and go/parser show. The ROADMAP's Tier A band is 0.2-2 s/1000 and gives toml no specific figure; this is roughly 4x below the floor of that band and the cheapest oracle in the repo, but the throughput number is the honest one to compare.
oracle_conformance: 712/712 against toml-lang/toml-test's TOML 1.1.0 expectations, and 21/21 on a hand-built encoding and whitespace battery (BOM alone / BOM x LF / BOM x CRLF, CRLF inside and outside multi-line strings, lone CR, no final newline, empty and whitespace-only documents, NUL and form feed in comments and strings, tab as the one permitted control character, non-BMP literals, \U0010FFFF vs \U00110000, lone surrogate, Latin-1 bytes in comments and strings). Both populations were needed and neither bounds the other: toml-test covers BOMs thoroughly and the real corpus contains none, while toml-test is blind to file-size distribution. The tbyaml session hit the mirror image — its suite has zero BOM cases while its corpus caught one — which is why each population records what it is blind to.

evidence.note: Prepends the redistribution warning to upstream's README. Touches no grammar code, so no sweep numbers move.

Upstream publishes as tree-sitter-toml-ng and does NOT own tree-sitter-toml on crates.io (that name belongs to Mathspy/tree-sitter-toml). Renames to treebank-grammar-toml and pins [lib] name = tree_sitter_toml_ng, which upstream leaves implicit — cargo derives it from the package name, so the rename would otherwise silently rename the library and break every consumer. Verified by building: emits libtree_sitter_toml_ng.rlib.

grammar_accepts_invalid.summary: Measured with the repo's OWN parse check (Node::has_error, which sweep.rs and `treebank negative` both use): the grammar accepts 86 of toml-test's 492 invalid files and correctly rejects 406 (82.5%). Recorded up front because this is the direction GRAMMARS.md names as where agents drift, and a sweep can never see it — a sweep only looks at files the grammar FAILED.
grammar_accepts_invalid.measurement_trap: An earlier version of this entry said 132 of 777 and was WRONG, because it used `tree-sitter parse`'s EXIT STATUS. That status ignores MISSING nodes, so a file the grammar 'parses' only by inserting a phantom token counts as accepted. has_error() counts ERROR and MISSING both. The three cases below are exactly the ones the two disagree on. Anyone measuring a grammar's rejection power must use has_error(), not the CLI's exit code — they are different questions and only one of them is the one the sweep asks.
grammar_accepts_invalid.how_much_is_structural: 59 of the 86 are semantic and unreachable for ANY tree-sitter grammar: table redefinition and duplicate keys (30), inline-table duplicate/overwrite (14), key duplicate and dotted-redefine (11), array extend-defined-aot and extending-table (4). A grammar cannot hold a symbol table.
grammar_accepts_invalid.datetime_validity: 13 more are calendar validity: feb-29/feb-30 on datetime, local-date and local-datetime; y10k (year > 9999); a 3-digit year; leading-zero dates. Partly reachable — the year-range and leading-zero cases are regex-expressible in rfc3339_date and are patch candidates; February 30th needs real calendar logic and probably belongs in a scanner if anywhere.
grammar_accepts_invalid.genuinely_syntactic: 14 are plain syntax the grammar should reject and is the patch queue: out-of-range Unicode escapes such as \U00110000 in basic and multiline strings (4), bad Unicode escapes (2), literal- and basic-multiline quote handling (3), and five spec-1.1.0 common cases. The out-of-range escape group is the cheapest — one bound on the \U rule covers four files.
grammar_accepts_invalid.not_a_gap: None of this can inflate gap_files: a gap is grammar-rejects + oracle-valid, and this is the opposite direction. It costs nothing in the sweep and everything in trustworthiness, which is why it is written down rather than left to be discovered.

test_negative.rule: PURE SYNTAX errors only, invalid under BOTH TOML 1.0.0 and 1.1.0, and verified rejected by the grammar via has_error().
test_negative.why_both_revisions: The oracle is 1.1.0. A 1.1.0-only construct is oracle-VALID, so it cannot enter by the stated criterion — and if it could, it would freeze this grammar at 1.0.0 and make a future upgrade fail CI. See spec_revision_choice.
test_negative.why_not_semantic: Duplicate keys, table redefinition, dotted-key conflicts and calendar-invalid datetimes are all oracle-invalid, but the grammar cannot reject them and by its nature never will. A negative test built from one would be testing the oracle, not the grammar. Same rule treebank-lua reached about scope errors.
test_negative.verified: Each of the 32 was checked against three things independently: toml 1.1.4 (invalid), toml 0.8.23 (invalid), and the repo's own has_error() check via `treebank negative` (rejects). Three of them — a leading comma in an array, two pairs on one line, and a UTF-16LE document — are the cases where `tree-sitter parse`'s exit status and has_error() disagree; they are in the corpus because has_error(), which is what the sweep uses, rejects all three.

corpus.source: crates.io .crate tarballs for the top 3000 crates by all-time downloads. TOML owns no registry — it is a GUEST language, like bash inside Debian sources — so the corpus rides inside another ecosystem's packages and the ranking is rust's, delegated rather than reimplemented.
corpus.ranking: crates.io database dump (corpus/rust/db), the same four CSVs treebank-rust reads; the dump is the only public source of all-time download counts.
corpus.files_note: .toml only, the single extension tree-sitter-toml's tree-sitter.json claims. Deliberately narrower than the editors: Helix additionally routes Cargo.lock, poetry.lock, pdm.lock, uv.lock and eight *.conf globs to this grammar and they are all really TOML. Excluded so classify() matches what the grammar advertises, and because a lock file is machine-generated output that would swamp the hand-written files with one template. Adding them is a deliberate change with its own sweep evidence — the call treebank-lua made about .rockspec.
corpus.composition_warning: 2969 of the 4034 files (73.6%) are cargo-normalized Cargo.toml — machine-generated by ONE program from ONE template, and stylistically identical. Only 1065 are hand-written (rustfmt.toml, clippy.toml, deny.toml, rust-toolchain.toml, config.toml, release.toml, and the test fixtures of TOML libraries). A clean sweep over this corpus is therefore weak evidence on its own, and the conformance suite and negative corpus carry most of the verification weight here. Stated because a 99.06% pass rate reads as reassurance and this corpus has not earned that much of it.
corpus.blind_to: Measured zeros across the whole corpus: no file starts with a BOM, none contains ill-formed UTF-8, a NUL, a lone CR or tab indentation. Those cases are covered only by toml-test and by the hand-built encoding battery. The reverse also holds — toml-test is blind to file-size distribution and to cargo-normalized output — which is why oracle.considered records what each population cannot see.

sweep_upstream.note: upstream 64b56832 with the two packaging patches only; no grammar patch has landed, so this is both the before and the current state. 99.06% of files parse.

corpus.every_failure_is_one_package: All 38 failures come from a single package: basic-toml 0.1.10, and specifically from its own tests/invalid/ and tests/valid/ fixture directories. basic-toml is a TOML parser crate, so it ships a conformance corpus, and 35 of the 38 are files it deliberately labels invalid. This is the phenomenon DESIGN.md opens with — corpora are full of test fixtures — appearing in its purest form: 2999 of 3000 packages parse completely clean and the entire failure surface belongs to the one package whose job is to contain broken TOML.

the_three_gaps.summary: TWO of the three gaps are the 1.1.0 oracle pin doing exactly what it was chosen to do, and the third is a genuine grammar bug. This is the ledger's spec_revision_choice prediction coming true on the first deepened sweep, so it is recorded in full.
the_three_gaps.gap_1_and_2_are_the_spec_gap: basic-toml tests/invalid/string-byte-escapes.toml (`answer = "\x33"`) and tests/invalid/datetime-malformed-no-secs.toml (`no-secs = 1987-07-05T17:45Z`). Both are VALID under TOML 1.1.0 and INVALID under 1.0.0 — \x byte escapes and optional seconds are two of the nine constructs that separate the revisions. Verified against both oracles: toml 1.1.4 says valid, toml 0.8.23 says invalid. A 1.0.0 oracle would have agreed with the grammar, booked both as noise, and reported a flawless grammar. The 1.1.0 pin is what makes them visible, and the correct response is a grammar patch bringing tree-sitter-toml to 1.1.0 — NOT a reclassification and NOT a swap back to 1.0.0. Note the irony worth keeping: basic-toml itself labels these files invalid, correctly, because it is a 1.0.0 parser published before 1.1.0 existed. The corpus's own labelling and our oracle disagree for a principled reason, which is precisely what the `spec` field exists to record.
the_three_gaps.gap_3_is_a_real_bug: basic-toml tests/valid/multiline-string.toml, line 11. A multi-line basic string using the line-ending backslash escape (`"""\` followed by whitespace and a continuation) and the empty form `""""""`. Valid under BOTH revisions — toml 1.1.4 and toml 0.8.23 both say valid — so this is an unambiguous defect in the grammar's multi-line string handling and is independent of the spec choice. It is the same defect the pre-vendoring conformance run found as valid/string/ends-in-whitespace-escape.toml and valid/string/multiline-empty.toml. First patch target.
the_three_gaps.prediction_recorded_before_the_sweep: spec_revision_choice.cost_today said gap_files was 0 on the 1374-file corpus and that a non-zero result would mean a real package had adopted 1.1.0 syntax, with a grammar patch as the correct response. Deepening 1000 -> 3000 packages produced exactly that.
